Good morning, Mr Brandt! I'm off today. I want to go to Museum Island. What's the best way to get there?
Ah, Museum Island! It's very easy. Take the M1! The stop is on the corner, next to the pharmacy.
The M1, of course! And where do I get off?

No, the M1 goes direct. I've done that route ten thousand times!

No, only five minutes on foot. Cross the bridge, then straight ahead. The Pergamon Museum is right there on the right, opposite the canal.

Once again: “eu” = “oy”. Haltestelle, Straße, Brücke have other traps: the “ü” in Brücke and the “ß” in Straße.
When “st” appears at the start of the second word in a compound, it's also read “sht”: Halte-stelle = “HAL-teh-shteh-leh”. But in the middle of a simple word it's read “st”: Fenster.
At the end of a word they become “voiceless”: ab = “ap”, Rad = “raht”, Weg = “vayk”.
The “ä” in “Nähe” is long, and in “Ämter” it's short; both sound like an open “e”, as in “bed”.
The imperative has three forms, depending on who you're talking to:
With “du”: verbs with e → i keep the “i” (nimm, iss, sprich, lies), but verbs with a → ä DON'T keep the umlaut: fahren → Fahr!, schlafen → Schlaf!
SEIN is irregular: Sei brav! (du) · Seid ruhig! (ihr) · Seien Sie vorsichtig! (Sie).
Add “bitte” or “doch mal” to make it sound friendlier: “Komm doch mal mit!” = Come on, come along!

Prepositions that ALWAYS take the dative (learn them like a poem: “aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber”):
mit dem Bus, mit der U-Bahn
